subject: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values

messages.author: 6b0398f60fd2d0a1
messages.subject: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
I'm working with collaborators and we've run into an odd error that persists even after updating to lava an 0.5-15

Here are two models:

mod1<-'
#model: box~arrows coming in
live.tree ~ Mean_T + Ann_Prec + Tppt.int + Drain + Drain2 + age + age2.100 + CWM_WD_TREE.10 + CWM_WD_TREE2
CWM_WD_TREE.10 ~ Mean_T + Ann_Prec + Tppt.int + Drain + 0*Drain2 + age + age2.100
'

mod2<-'
#model: box~arrows coming in
live.tree ~ Mean_T + Ann_Prec + Tppt.int + Drain + Drain2 + age + age2.100 + CWM_WD_TREE.10 + CWM_WD_TREE2
'


Let's focus on live.tree as our response variable. Both models produce identical unstandardized coefficients which are pretty much the same as if you did a multiple linear regression.

However, if we call summary on the fits, and set rsq=2 we get radically different rsquare values

For the model WITH CWM_WD_TREE.10 as a response variable (mod1) the live.tree R^2 = 0.944. For mod2, which is just a multiple linear regression, the live.tree R^2 is 0.366.

The residual variances are also the same between the two models.

What is going on here that would produce such radically different R^2 values?

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
On 11/22/2013 11:29 PM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> Here's a reproducible example with data. Note how the R^2 value for y2
> changes.
Thanks. This helps. But I don't think anything is wrong here.

I think it has something to do with the 0* for the second
> predictor in mod2

You get the same result if you omit the 0*x term. You can already see
the difference if you request the standardized solution:

library(lavaan)
set.seed(2002)
adf <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), x1 = rnorm(100), y1 = rnorm(100), y2 =
rnorm(100))

mod1 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1 '

fit1 <- sem(mod1, adf)
fit2 <- sem(mod2, adf)

summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)

Variances:
y2 0.743 0.105 0.743 0.935

summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)

Variances:
y2 0.743 0.105 0.743 0.923


But in mod1, 'y1' is simply an exogenous variable; while in mod2, 'y1'
is not exogenous anymore, since it is the dependent variable in the
second equation.
In the 'Std.all' column, the regression parameters are standardized
based on the variances (or residual variances) of the observed
variables; however, this number is not the same for 'y1' in both models.
Hence the difference.

(PS: the resid(fit, "casewise") function has been fixed in 0.5-15 and
should now work correctly with exogenous variables)

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
On 11/23/2013 12:17 AM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> I see what you're saying about y1, but why is the R^2 for y2
> changing?
Because in the first case, R^2 is based on the regression
y2 ~ x + x1 + y1

while the second case, R^2 is based on the regression

y2 ~ x + x1 + y1bis

where y1bis is the residual of 'y1 ~ x1', not y1 itself.

Yves.

messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
While I see where you're coming from, I still am missing something.  True, in the regression example, the big difference is that y1 and x are allowed to covary.  Not so in the 2 equation example. This is why they differ by 1df. Indeed, a similar model:

mod3 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1; y1 ~~ 0*x +x1; x ~~ x1'
fit3 <- sem(mod3, adf, fixed.x=F)

Produced the same R2 results as mod2. So, it's a function of no longer allowing x and y1 covary.  OK, I see that, but...

But that shouldn't matter.  With R2 = 1-residual variance / observed variance, if the estimate of the residual variance is the same (and it is in all models) for y2, the R2 value should also be the same. Unless it is a different formula being used here.

r2.lavaan <- function(obj){
  fit <- diag(inspect(obj, "coef")$psi)

}

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
The confusion seems to stem from the formula that is used to compute the
R^2.

R^2 of a dependent variable (say, y2), is 1 minus the (estimated)
standardized residual variance for y2. In our example:

set.seed(2002)
adf <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), x1=rnorm(100), y1=rnorm(100), y2=rnorm(100))

fit1 <- sem(mod1, data=adf)
fit2 <- sem(mod2, data=adf)
summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)
summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)

For fit1, we get (see last column):

Estimate Std.err Z-value P(>|z|) Std.lv Std.all

while for fit2, we get

Estimate Std.err Z-value P(>|z|) Std.lv Std.all

So we need to explain how we compute the 'Std.all' value for y2 in both
settings.

We need to compute the model-implied variances for each model, and this
is where we see the differences (see first element 'y2'):

> diag( fitted(fit1)$cov )
y2 x x1 y1
0.7948851 1.0103473 0.9897522 0.8568083

> diag( fitted(fit2)$cov )
y2 y1 x x1
0.8051950 0.8568084 1.0103473 0.9897522

Dividing the original estimate (0.743) by either 0.7948851 or 0.8051950
gives the two Std.all versions.

Why are the fitted variances different? Because in mod2, we have a
non-zero regression coefficient in the beta matrix (for y2 ~ x1), and
this affects the corresponding element in 'psi' matrix, and evenutally
the model implied (co)variances. Since we have no latent variables, the
model-implied covariance matrix is given by

solve(diag(4)-beta) %*% psi %*% t( solve(diag(4)-beta) )

Both beta and psi are a bit different in the two models. but it is the
psi matrix that makes the difference.

> inspect(fit1, "est")[3:4]
$psi
y2 x x1 y1
y2 0.743
x 0.000 1.010
x1 0.000 -0.035 0.990
y1 0.000 0.154 0.017 0.857

$beta
y2 x x1 y1
y2 0 0.181 -0.001 -0.184
x 0 0.000 0.000 0.000
x1 0 0.000 0.000 0.000
y1 0 0.000 0.000 0.000

> inspect(fit2, "est")[3:4]
$psi
y2 y1 x x1
y2 0.743
y1 0.000 0.857
x 0.000 0.000 1.010
x1 0.000 0.000 -0.035 0.990

$beta
y2 y1 x x1
y2 0 -0.184 0.181 -0.001
y1 0 0.000 0.000 0.017
x 0 0.000 0.000 0.000
x1 0 0.000 0.000 0.000



Yves.

messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
Right, whereas I (and I'm going to guess many other folk) are more interested in the squared multiple correlation (R^2smc in Kline p. 160) which uses the disturbance estimate divided by the observed total variance. This is often more in line with what folk are talking about when they go variable by variable, as there interested in predictive power of the equations, and it's what the function I sent gets at. Particularly when users are dealing with observed variable only models.

Hrm.

I suppose both could be reported? They should often be the same except in cases of very different model structure, yes?

Thoughts?

parts:
On 12/05/2013 05:52 PM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> Right, whereas I (and I'm going to guess many other folk) are more
> interested in the squared multiple correlation (R^2smc in Kline p.
> 160) which uses the disturbance estimate divided by the observed
> total variance.

Like you say, many people (including Kline) seem to expect that the
'regression' formula for R2 simply translates to the SEM setting. In my
book, the model-based approach makes more sense (in a SEM).

Anyway, I will see if I can provide both options (unfortunately, this is
not trivial, since I need to tinker with the standardization code).

But, remember that SEM is a model-based game. We first aim to fit the
data well. Then, perhaps, we may look at predictive power. Not the other
way around. If the model fits well, the model-implied variances will be
very close -if not identical- to the observed variances, and all is
well. If the model doesn't fit well, I would not even bother looking at
the R-square values...

Yves.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
parts:
Yves--
     I agree with you that the formula:

R2 = 1 - residual variance / observed total variance

sounds like a bad combination of empirical and model-implied terms.  But if, instead of "observed total variance," you used a model-implied total variance (a function of parameter estimates), then you could avoid the negative consequences of relying on standardized parameter estimates.
     If the model is misspecified, then yes, it hardly matters how you compute R2.
--Ed Rigdon
